title: Stormline batching fidelity vs cost vignette
content:
Purpose

Quick sketch + working notes to capture an experiment family we ran in early May: "stormline" workload (dense microbursts with variable session fidelity) and how different batching heuristics trade latency tail vs unit cost. Not polished — notes to self and a suggested follow-up plan.

Context and why this matters

- We frequently see customer workloads that are mostly low throughput but have frequent short-lived microbursts (mobile assistants, chat widgets, autosuggest).
- Existing batchers that prioritize packing for token-efficiency (aggressive-fill) increase amortization but can introduce p99/jank for callers that expect session-level prompt+reply coherence (we call that "fidelity" — minimizing reordering, low intra-session latency).
- This vignette looks at three heuristic families and shows simple ASCII charts of observed tradeoffs. Goal: decide which heuristics to prototype in console as recommended presets (interactive, balanced, cost-first).

Workload definition: "stormline"

- Duration: 30m runs across five replicated hosts.
- Session arrival: Poisson baseline (0.2 qps per host) + injected microbursts: every 30s a 4–12 req burst lasting 300–900ms.
- Message size: prompt=80 tokens, expected generative tokens=32 (median) with heavy tail to 256.
- Session fidelity constraint: prefer same-session request to be scheduled within 120ms if possible. If not, it's considered a fidelity miss (user-perceivable jank).

Heuristics compared

1) aggressive-fill (AF): hold up to 10ms to accumulate inputs and fill GPU batch slots to 100% occupancy; LIFO pack to maximize utilization.
2) session-cohere (SC): prefer grouping by session; will wait up to 60ms for same-session ops and otherwise dispatch partially filled slots.
3) hybrid-threshold (HT): adaptive wait: if recent miss-rate < 2% then act like AF; if fidelity misses > 1% escalate to SC for next 1s.

Key metrics we recorded (per-host aggregated)

- median-latency (ms)
- p95, p99 (ms)
- tokens-per-dollar (k tokens / $)
- fidelity-miss-rate (%)
- GPU-occupancy (%) measured by kernel active time fraction

Representative results (ASCII summary — numbers rounded):

+----------------------+----------+--------+--------+-----------------+
| heuristic            | p99(ms)  | p95   | tokens/$| fidelity-miss%  |
+----------------------+----------+--------+--------+-----------------+
| aggressive-fill (AF) | 820      | 210    | 125k   | 9.4             |
| session-cohere (SC)  | 420      | 240    | 88k    | 1.1             |
| hybrid-threshold (HT)| 480      | 230    | 110k   | 2.8             |
+----------------------+----------+--------+--------+-----------------+

Observations and interpretation

- AF gives best tokens/$ by ~40% vs SC because of near-perfect packing during bursts, but p99 is terrible (long tails) and fidelity miss rate is high — not acceptable for interactive UX.
- SC improves p99 substantially and reduces fidelity misses to near-target, but sacrifices packing efficiency which raises unit cost. Median is similar across heuristics (user-facing median latency is dominated by model runtime rather than batching), but tails differ.
- HT is a pragmatic middle ground: still loses some tokens/$ vs AF but recovers most fidelity. The adaptive rule dampens oscillations in bursty windows more gracefully than a static threshold.

Text chart: tokens/$ vs p99 tradeoff (lower-left is better: low p99, high tokens/$). Approx points:

AF: (tokens/$=125k, p99=820)
SC: (tokens/$=88k, p99=420)
HT: (tokens/$=110k, p99=480)

Simple decision matrix (for product presets)

- interactive (preset): session-cohere recommended. Rationale: favors p99 and fidelity; acceptable cost for consumer-facing assistants.
- balanced (preset): hybrid-threshold recommended. Rationale: good mix, auto-adapts across burst intensity.
- cost-first (preset): aggressive-fill but with explicit UX warning and per-route SLA opt-out. Rationale: for batchy workloads or when customers accept degraded tail for better cost.

Micro-insights and anomalies

- We observed a secondary tail mode in AF: requests that hit the long tail almost always coincided with cross-session packing where a single large-generation (>=200 tokens) blocked the GPU pipeline; we should consider response-chunking escape-hatch (send partial stream and release slots) to reduce worst-case p99.
- SC sometimes underutilizes cold VMs when burst intensity is extremely low (most packets singletons) — we lose occupancy but fidelity is preserved. HT mitigates but requires a tuned hysteresis window; 1s was a sweet spot in these runs.
- Tokens/$ sensitivity to model size: for small models (<=7B) the occupancy advantage translates less into tokens/$ because CPU/IO factors become higher fraction. For large models (>30B) AF wins more on dollars but worsens p99 more dramatically. Need model-size aware presets.

Open questions to resolve (next experiments)

- Sweep HT hysteresis: 250ms, 500ms, 1s, 2s — measure oscillation amplitude and energy efficiency.
- Add chunked-stream fallback: when a gen > 128 tokens detected, fast-path stream-first-chunk then continue packing remaining tokens as a separate op. Does that cut AF p99 by >30% without losing >5% tokens/$?
- Evaluate with realistic client RTTs: these runs assumed negligible network latency; real-world mobile RTTs could push effective wait budgets down.
- Add cost-of-jank metric: quantify user dropoff or business cost per fidelity miss (need PM/UX input).

Suggested immediate actions (concrete)

- Prototype HT in tiling-sim repo (PR referenced above) with configurable hysteresis and stream-first parameter. Assign to Miguel (1 week) for a baseline microbenchmark.
- Add a console preset draft page: interactive / balanced / cost-first (copyable route config + short description + when to use). Draft by Asha -> review Lin (end of week).
- Run model size sweep for small, medium, large (7B / 13B / 70B) with HT hysteresis at 500ms and 1s to collect tokens/$ sensitivity. Samir to own (2 weeks).

Loose notes / friction points

- Telemetry: fidelity-miss is currently not a tracked metric in the console; need a lightweight event (fidelity_miss boolean) emitted by scheduler. Engineering-sre + SDK owners need to agree on stable name and cost overhead.
- Billing mapping: tokens/$ currently derived from offline cost model; if we recommend presets, ops wants to see expected bill delta per preset per 100k requests. Add that to the preset pages.

Appendix: raw-ish ASCII latency distribution excerpts (single host, stormline run)

p50: 170ms (all heuristics converge)
p75: AF=195ms, SC=205ms, HT=200ms
p90: AF=260ms, SC=270ms, HT=265ms
p95: AF=210ms (see table above — artifacts from binning),
p99: AF long tail 700–900ms (multi-modal); SC 380–460ms; HT 440–520ms

Closing thought

This sketch demonstrates the value of exposing scheduler presets with clear UX tradeoffs rather than a single-one-size-fits-all optimizer. For customer conversations, framing as "latency-fidelity budget" (percent expected fidelity misses per 100k calls) + expected tokens/$ delta will be a clearer commercial story than raw occupancy numbers.

-- Asha
